families.title: Positive lower density of large prime gaps
families.headline: **026. Positive lower density of large prime gaps.** For every fixed C > 0, a positive proportion of consecutive prime gaps exceed $`C\log p_n`$, throughout every sufficiently large initial segment of the primes. The proportion may depend on C. Consequently, the indices where $`p_n/n`$ increases have positive lower density, answering Erdős and Prachar. ([Lean](lean/docs/026.md))

clauses.note: Only in a weaker form: the count of n in [1, N] with C·log p_n < p_{n+1} − p_n is bounded below by c·√N, not c·N. A count of order √N is compatible with density zero, so 'a positive proportion' is not stated.

clauses.coveredBy: ∃ N₀ : ℕ, ∀ N : ℕ, N₀ ≤ N → (line 38), over Finset.Icc 1 N (line 11)
clauses.note: The quantifier form is right; it carries the weakened √N count.

clauses.clause: The proportion may depend on C
clauses.note: Right order: c and N₀ are chosen after C.

clauses.clause: Consequently, the indices where p_n/n increases have positive lower density
clauses.coveredBy: second conjunct, line 40; ratioIncreaseIndices (lines 31-34); lowerAsymptoticDensity (lines 27-29)
clauses.note: Stated in full: n ≥ 1 with p_n/n < p_{n+1}/(n+1), p_n = Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n − 1) so p_1 = 2; the sSup of eventual lower bounds of count/N is the liminf, and 0 < liminf is positive lower density.

clauses.coveredBy: same as the previous clause

families.gap: The headline's main clause (for every C > 0, at least c·N of the first N gaps exceed C log p_n) is stated only as a c·√N lower bound (challenge.lean:39). The ratio corollary, which only concerns gaps above p_n/n ≈ log p_n (C about 1), does not recover it for C > 1. The corollary itself is stated in full.

The note gives the formal scope as the corollary alone and names the large-gap theorem as the paper's; its only comparator row is 'Positive lower density of prime-ratio increases'.

families.suspicious: I disagree with the first reader's NARROWER — UNDECLARED. The gap (√N against N) is certain. The word depends on whether the scope note declares it, and I read that it does: the Scope section says what the formalized supplement proves (the ratio corollary) and calls it the corollary of 'the paper's theorem', so it places the large-gap theorem outside the formal scope. The declaration is implicit, not a 'not included' sentence, and the note never mentions the extra √N conjunct. A reader who gives weight to the theorem name may still say UNDECLARED.

families.title: The Kadison–Ringrose cohomology conjecture
families.headline: **295. The Kadison–Ringrose cohomology conjecture.** Proves that every bounded Hochschild cocycle of degree at least two on a complex von Neumann algebra, with coefficients in the algebra itself, has a bounded primitive. Equivalently, all higher bounded Hochschild cohomology groups vanish, resolving the Kadison–Ringrose conjecture. ([Lean](lean/docs/295.md))

clauses.coveredBy: f : Cochain M (n + 2) (ContinuousMultilinearMap, lines 12-13) with hf : δf = 0 (line 33)
clauses.note: Matches: degree n + 2 ≥ 2. The differential (lines 15-24) has the standard signs: a_0 f(...), (−1)^{j+1} on the merge of positions j, j+1, (−1)^{n+1} on f(...)·a_n.

clauses.clause: on a complex von Neumann algebra
clauses.coveredBy: [CStarAlgebra M] [PartialOrder M] [StarOrderedRing M] [WStarAlgebra M] [TopologicalSpace.SeparableSpace M] (lines 31-32)
clauses.note: NARROWER: SeparableSpace M is about the only topology in scope, the norm topology. An infinite-dimensional von Neumann algebra has an infinite family of orthogonal projections, and the sums over subsets give uncountably many projections at mutual norm distance 1, so it is never norm-separable. The statement covers only finite-dimensional W*-algebras.

clauses.clause: with coefficients in the algebra itself
clauses.coveredBy: Cochain M n takes values in M; δ uses the left action v 0 * … and the right action … * v (Fin.last n) (lines 22, 24)
clauses.note: Matches.

clauses.clause: has a bounded primitive

clauses.note: Matches.

clauses.clause: Equivalently, all higher bounded Hochschild cohomology groups vanish, resolving the Kadison–Ringrose conjecture
clauses.coveredBy: same as above
clauses.note: Only for norm-separable, i.e. finite-dimensional, algebras, where vanishing is classical (semisimple finite-dimensional algebras have vanishing Hochschild cohomology in degrees ≥ 1).

families.gap: The headline covers every complex von Neumann algebra. The statement adds [TopologicalSpace.SeparableSpace M] (challenge.lean:32) for the norm topology, which restricts it to finite-dimensional algebras. The scope note says the opposite: 'No separability or type restriction is imposed.'
families.asserts: For every complex W*-algebra M that is separable in its norm topology, every n, and every bounded (n+2)-linear Hochschild cocycle f : M^{n+2} → M with coefficients in M, there is a bounded (n+1)-linear g with δg = f.

families.title: Boolean functions violate the square-root degree bound by arbitrary factors
families.headline: **192. Boolean functions violate the square-root degree bound by arbitrary factors.** Disproves the proposed square-root bound relating a Boolean function's linear Fourier coefficients to its polynomial degree. For every C > 0, there is a sign-valued Boolean function f with $`\sum_i\widehat f(\{i\})\gt C\sqrt{\deg(f)}`$. Thus its total signed correlation with individual input bits can exceed the proposed bound by an arbitrary factor. ([Lean](lean/docs/192.md))

clauses.clause: For every C > 0
clauses.coveredBy: ∀ C : ℝ, 0 < C → (line 47)
clauses.note: Matches.

clauses.clause: there is a sign-valued Boolean function f
clauses.coveredBy: ∃ n, 0 < n ∧ ∃ f : Cube (Fin n) → ℝ, IsBoolean f ∧ Nonconstant f (lines 47-48), IsBoolean f := ∀ x, |f x| ≤ 1 (lines 34-35)
clauses.note: NARROWER: IsBoolean only bounds the outputs by 1 in absolute value; f need not be ±1-valued. The comment at lines 6-7 concerns the inputs (Bool encodes a sign).

clauses.clause: with Σ_i f̂({i}) > C√deg(f)
clauses.coveredBy: C * Real.sqrt (fourierDegree f) < singletonSum f (line 48), uniform-average Fourier coefficients and real Fourier degree (lines 20-32, 40-41)
clauses.note: The inequality and the degree notion match; the class of f is wider.

clauses.clause: Thus its total signed correlation with individual input bits can exceed the proposed bound by an arbitrary factor
clauses.coveredBy: same as above
clauses.note: Covered for [−1,1]-valued f, not for Boolean f.

families.gap: The headline asks for a sign-valued (±1) Boolean function; the statement only requires |f x| ≤ 1 (challenge.lean:35). For bounded functions the violation is elementary: f = T_d((x_1+…+x_n)/n) with T_d the Chebyshev polynomial (odd d) is [−1,1]-valued, has degree ≤ d, and level-one sum → T_d'(0) = ±d as n → ∞, far above C√d. The square-root conjecture is about Boolean functions, and the statement does not reach it. The second conjunct is also over bounded f.
families.asserts: (i) For every C > 0 there is a nonconstant f : {±1}^n → [−1,1] (n > 0) with Σ_i f̂({i}) > C·√deg f; (ii) the ratios Σ_i |f̂({i})| / √deg f over [−1,1]-valued f of positive degree are unbounded above.
encoding: Bool input encoded as a sign (false ↦ +1, true ↦ −1)
Fourier coefficients against the uniform average
degree = largest |s| with a nonzero real Fourier coefficient

flags: IsBoolean is a misnomer: it means bounded, not sign-valued.
Headline ⟹ statement (±1-valued is bounded; a witness is automatically nonconstant), so the word is NARROWER, not DIFFERENT.
Nonconstant forces a nonzero coefficient at some nonempty s, so deg f > 0 and √deg f > 0; no junk.
The Chebyshev example is a sketch; the word rests on the definition of IsBoolean alone.

families.title: Cycle–clique Ramsey numbers
families.headline: **189. Cycle–clique Ramsey numbers.** Proves the Erdős–Faudree–Rousseau–Schelp conjecture: $`R(C_m,K_n)=(m-1)(n-1)+1`$ for every $`m\ge n\ge3`$, except $`R(C_3,K_3)=6`$. This is the exact threshold forcing a red m-cycle or a blue n-clique in every red–blue coloring of a complete graph. ([Lean](lean/docs/189.md))

families.title: Riesz transforms and rectifiability in higher codimension
families.headline: **081. Riesz transforms and rectifiability in higher codimension.** Resolves the remaining higher-codimension Riesz-transform rectifiability problem: for d ≥ 4 and $`2\le n\le d-2`$, an n-Ahlfors–David regular Radon measure on ℝd is uniformly n-rectifiable whenever its n-dimensional Riesz transform is uniformly L2-bounded over all positive hard truncations. The rectifiability bounds depend only on dimension, regularity and operator bounds. ([Lean](lean/docs/081.md))

families.title: A counterexample to periodic tiling in dimension three
families.headline: **155. A counterexample to periodic tiling in dimension three.** Constructs a finite translational tile in ℤ<sup>3</sup> that tiles space but admits no fully periodic tiling, disproving the periodic tiling conjecture in the smallest possible lattice dimension. Its unit-cube thickening gives the same counterexample in ℝ<sup>3</sup>, even with arbitrary real translation vectors. ([Lean](lean/docs/155.md))

families.title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
families.headline: **173. Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture.** Proves Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture: every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex with at least as many vertices at directed distance exactly two as at directed distance one. Oriented graphs may be arbitrary apart from the exclusion of loops and oppositely directed edge pairs. ([Lean](lean/docs/173.md))
